The margin for making diesel from crude oil in the US has soared to more than $100 a barrel, setting new all-time highs as a global fuel-making crunch continues to exacerbate fuel prices.

The widely watched gauge, known as the diesel crack spread, hovered around $100 a barrel on Tuesday down slightly from record highs over $102 a barrel. The spread settled in triple digits for the first time on Monday.

Before this year, the measure had never risen above $89 a barrel, with the prior record set in October 2022 as the world grappled with a shortage of the fuel heading into the first winter of the Russia-Ukraine war.

Great point.

If the admin wants to onshore and re-engineer the entire supply chain per their playbook, refining and smelting remain the critical choke point. 

China owns the midstream processing moat, and the US is completely flat footed. Building out midstream capacity chews up infinitely more capex and lead time than simply stacking upstream stockpiles. 

And for this to be structurally viable, unit economics need to make sense—and running a smelter stateside is basically signing up for structural negative margins.

None of this pencils out without massive, permanent federal backstops, and I’m deeply skeptical of the US's follow through post-Liberation Day. 

How many times do we need to see Beijing weaponize the critical minerals and rare earths tape before we learn...?

Broad #commodities: The BCOM TR index has rebounded 13.2% from its late-June correction low and now trades just 3.2% below the record high reached in May. Importantly, the recovery has been broad-based, with all major sectors posting gains. Energy and soft commodities lead with gains of 20% and 19.5%, respectively, followed by grains at 12.4% and precious metals at 10.5%, while industrial metals lag with a still-solid 6.8% advance.

At the individual commodity level, the strongest gains have been concentrated in energy, where London gasoil (diesel) has surged 55%, EU natural gas 53% (not a BCOM component) and US diesel 46%, highlighting continued tightness across refined products and regional gas markets. Brent and WTI have both risen around 23%, while gasoline is up 22.5%. Outside energy, coffee has gained 22.5%, sugar 21% and cocoa 20.5%. Wheat, cotton and corn have all risen around 13%, while silver has outperformed gold, gaining 12.3% versus 10.1%. US natural gas stands out as the only contract in the group trading lower, down 17.2% since the correction low.

Overall, the BCOMTR trades up around 28% YTD and 42% during the past 12 months. There are numerous ETFs track or seek to replicate the performance of index, with the Invesco Bloomberg Commodity UCITS ETF (CMOD) among the largest in terms of market capitalisation.

Investor concerns about the US fiscal and debt outlook are also providing support, particularly as long-end Treasury yields continue to rise.
